# California’s new incentive program could cause battery electric tractor-truck sales to skyrocket

July 27, 2026 | By: Jane O’Malley and Anish Sinha

Tractor trucks account for roughly 1% of all registered motor vehicles but are responsible for [15%–20%](https://www.fhwa.dot.gov/policyinformation/statistics/2023/vm1.cfm) of on-road energy consumption, meaning electrifying this segment is critical for vehicle decarbonization. But ask a California fleet manager whether now is a good time to go electric, and you’ll get a complicated answer. The federal incentives they were counting on are gone: the Inflation Reduction Act’s tax credit for clean heavy-duty vehicles was canceled last year. But a new state program is trying to make electric trucks cheaper for fleets.

#### Federal cuts, state response

When it comes to electrifying heavy-duty vehicles, the upfront price gap is the core problem. [Our research](https://theicct.org/publication/battery-electric-commercial-vehicle-pricing-in-the-us-sept25/) has found that the average battery electric tractor-trailer in the United States sells for roughly 2.4 times the price of a diesel one. Battery electric vehicle (BEV) prices have come down for some vehicle classes, but they remain [stubbornly high](https://theicct.org/publication/battery-electric-commercial-vehicle-pricing-in-the-us-sept25/) for the workhorses California most needs to electrify: Class 8 tractor-trailers, used for everything from freight delivery to construction. Hauling heavy payloads takes bigger batteries, and bigger batteries cost more. [The arrival of](https://theicct.org/truck-electrification-at-a-crossroads-how-states-can-lead-it-in-the-right-direction-apr26/) the Tesla Semi at a retail price of $290,000 may signal a coming shift, but there is still a sizeable cost differential with [diesel models](https://theicct.org/publication/battery-electric-commercial-vehicle-pricing-in-the-us-sept25/), and fleets need help bridging the gap.

Until recently, federal incentives were helping to close the cost gap between diesel trucks and BEVs. Inflation Reduction Act tax credits offered up to [$40,000 in purchase rebates](https://www.irs.gov/credits-deductions/commercial-clean-vehicle-credit) for Class 4 vehicles and above before they were prematurely canceled at the end of September. That leaves state-level programs like California’s Clean Truck and Bus Voucher Incentive Project (HVIP) to do the heavy lifting. Since 2009, HVIP has awarded more than $1 billion in purchase rebates on a first-come, first-serve basis. Fleets are still sitting on more than [$570 million in unredeemed vouchers](https://californiahvip.org/#voucher

Since 2009, HVIP has awarded more than $1 billion in purchase rebates on a first-come, first-serve basis. # California’s new incentive program could cause battery electric tractor-truck sales to skyrocket

July 27, 2026 |
By: Jane O’Malley and Anish Sinha

Tractor trucks account for roughly 1% of all registered motor vehicles but are responsible for [15%–20%](https://www.fhwa.dot.gov/policyinformation/statistics/2023/vm1.cfm) of on-road energy consumption, meaning electrifying this segment is critical for vehicle decarbonization. But ask a California fleet manager whether now is a good time to go electric, and you’ll get a complicated answer. The federal incentives they were counting on are gone: the Inflation Reduction Act’s tax credit for clean heavy-duty vehicles was canceled last year. But a new state program is trying to make electric trucks cheaper for fleets.

#### Federal cuts, state response

When it comes to electrifying heavy-duty vehicles, the upfront price gap is the core problem. [Our research](https://theicct.org/publication/battery-electric-commercial-vehicle-pricing-in-the-us-sept25/) has found that the average battery electric tractor-trailer in the United States sells for roughly 2.4 times the price of a diesel one. Battery electric vehicle (BEV) prices have come down for some vehicle classes, but they remain [stubbornly high](https://theicct.org/publication/battery-electric-commercial-vehicle-pricing-in-the-us-sept25/) for the workhorses California most needs to electrify: Class 8 tractor-trailers, used for everything from freight delivery to construction. Hauling heavy payloads takes bigger batteries, and bigger batteries cost more. [The arrival of](https://theicct.org/truck-electrification-at-a-crossroads-how-states-can-lead-it-in-the-right-direction-apr26/) the Tesla Semi at a retail price of $290,000 may signal a coming shift, but there is still a sizeable cost differential with [diesel models](https://theicct.org/publication/battery-electric-commercial-vehicle-pricing-in-the-us-sept25/), and fleets need help bridging the gap.

Until recently, federal incentives were helping to close the cost gap between diesel trucks and BEVs. Inflation Reduction Act tax credits offered up to [$40,000 in purchase rebates](https://www.irs.gov/credits-deductions/commercial-clean-vehicle-credit) for Class 4 vehicles and above before they were prematurely canceled at the end of September. That leaves state-level programs like California’s Clean Truck and Bus Voucher Incentive Project (HVIP) to do the heavy lifting. Since 2009, HVIP has awarded more than $1 billion in purchase rebates on a first-come, first-serve basis. Fleets are still sitting on more than [$570 million in unredeemed vouchers](https://californiahvip.org/#voucher-map) from the latest funding round, which must be redeemed within the next 18 months—and 77% of those vouchers are earmarked for Class 8 BEVs.

To keep momentum on the heavy-duty side, California now plans to deploy [$1 billion](https://ww2.arb.ca.gov/news/california-launching-1-billion-rebate-program-electric-trucks) through a new [Clean Fuel Reward (CFR) program](https://ww2.arb.ca.gov/news/california-launching-1-billion-rebate-program-electric-trucks), funded by Low Carbon Fuel Standard (LCFS) credits from residential charging of electric vehicles. These point-of-sale rebates will help narrow the [total cost of ownership](https://theicct.org/the-economic-case-for-zevs-is-often-hidden-in-plain-sight-the-iccts-total-cost-of-ownership-calculator-reveals-it-mar26/) (TCO) gap between battery electric and diesel trucks. TCO is a key metric for fleet operators’ purchasing decisions that considers purchase price, infrastructure costs, operating costs, and resale value over a 3–5-year period.

#### Running the numbers

Using our recently published [TCO calculator](https://theicct.org/tco-calculator/#/?vehicle_class=89953&region=89964&charger_type=89950&charger_cost=40000&number_of_chargers=1&charger_maintenance=1000&infrastructure_useful_life=15&vehicle_purchase_price=65000&fuel_economy=15&maintenance_cost=0.14&be), we found that the 3-year TCO of an average battery electric tractor operating [80,000 miles per year](https://truckingresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/ATRI-Operational-Costs-of-Trucking-07-2025.pdf) in California is 98% higher than an equivalent diesel tractor without incentives in place. When assuming a $290,000 price tag in line with the [Tesla Semi](https://www.tesla.com/semi-charger-for-business/get) plus the comparatively cheaper cost of a Tesla charger ($20,000), the gap narrows to 44%.

Purchase incentives can flip the math for fleets that would otherwise pick diesel on cost alone. Using our baseline assumptions, reaching 3-year TCO parity today would require more than $330,000 in purchase incentives for Class 8 fleet operators. Lower-priced vehicles need less, because they start closer to parity. Figure 1 shows how HVIP base vouchers and CFR incentives stack up against the gap for all heavy-duty vehicle classes.

# California’s new incentive program could cause battery electric tractor-truck sales to skyrocket

July 27, 2026 |
By: Jane O’Malley and Anish Sinha

Tractor trucks account for roughly 1% of all registered motor vehicles but are responsible for [15%–20%](https://www.fhwa.dot.gov/policyinformation/statistics/2023/vm1.cfm) of on-road energy consumption, meaning electrifying this segment is critical for vehicle decarbonization. But ask a California fleet manager whether now is a good time to go electric, and you’ll get a complicated answer. The federal incentives they were counting on are gone: the Inflation Reduction Act’s tax credit for clean heavy-duty vehicles was canceled last year. But a new state program is trying to make electric trucks cheaper for fleets.

#### Federal cuts, state response

When it comes to electrifying heavy-duty vehicles, the upfront price gap is the core problem. [Our research](https://theicct.org/publication/battery-electric-commercial-vehicle-pricing-in-the-us-sept25/) has found that the average battery electric tractor-trailer in the United States sells for roughly 2.4 times the price of a diesel one. Battery electric vehicle (BEV) prices have come down for some vehicle classes, but they remain [stubbornly high](https://theicct.org/publication/battery-electric-commercial-vehicle-pricing-in-the-us-sept25/) for the workhorses California most needs to electrify: Class 8 tractor-trailers, used for everything from freight delivery to construction. Hauling heavy payloads takes bigger batteries, and bigger batteries cost more. [The arrival of](https://theicct.org/truck-electrification-at-a-crossroads-how-states-can-lead-it-in-the-right-direction-apr26/) the Tesla Semi at a retail price of $290,000 may signal a coming shift, but there is still a sizeable cost differential with [diesel models](https://theicct.org/publication/battery-electric-commercial-vehicle-pricing-in-the-us-sept25/), and fleets need help bridging the gap.

Until recently, federal incentives were helping to close the cost gap between diesel trucks and BEVs. Inflation Reduction Act tax credits offered up to [$40,000 in purchase rebates](https://www.irs.gov/credits-deductions/commercial-clean-vehicle-credit) for Class 4 vehicles and above before they were prematurely canceled at the end of September. That leaves state-level programs like California’s Clean Truck and Bus Voucher Incentive Project (HVIP) to do the heavy lifting. Since 2009, HVIP has awarded more than $1 billion in purchase rebates on a first-come, first-serve basis. Fleets are still sitting on more than [$570 million in unredeemed vouchers](https://californiahvip.org/#voucher-map) from the latest funding round, which must be redeemed within the next 18 months—and 77% of those vouchers are earmarked for Class 8 BEVs.

To keep momentum on the heavy-duty side, California now plans to deploy [$1 billion](https://ww2.arb.ca.gov/news/california-launching-1-billion-rebate-program-electric-trucks) through a new [Clean Fuel Reward (CFR) program](https://ww2.arb.ca.gov/news/california-launching-1-billion-rebate-program-electric-trucks), funded by Low Carbon Fuel Standard (LCFS) credits from residential charging of electric vehicles. These point-of-sale rebates will help narrow the [total cost of ownership](https://theicct.org/the-economic-case-for-zevs-is-often-hidden-in-plain-sight-the-iccts-total-cost-of-ownership-calculator-reveals-it-mar26/) (TCO) gap between battery electric and diesel trucks. TCO is a key metric for fleet operators’ purchasing decisions that considers purchase price, infrastructure costs, operating costs, and resale value over a 3–5-year period.

#### Running the numbers

Using our recently published [TCO calculator](https://theicct.org/tco-calculator/#/?vehicle_class=89953&region=89964&charger_type=89950&charger_cost=40000&number_of_chargers=1&charger_maintenance=1000&infrastructure_useful_life=15&vehicle_purchase_price=65000&fuel_economy=15&maintenance_cost=0.14&be), we found that the 3-year TCO of an average battery electric tractor operating [80,000 miles per year](https://truckingresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/ATRI-Operational-Costs-of-Trucking-07-2025.pdf) in California is 98% higher than an equivalent diesel tractor without incentives in place. When assuming a $290,000 price tag in line with the [Tesla Semi](https://www.tesla.com/semi-charger-for-business/get) plus the comparatively cheaper cost of a Tesla charger ($20,000), the gap narrows to 44%.

Purchase incentives can flip the math for fleets that would otherwise pick diesel on cost alone. Using our baseline assumptions, reaching 3-year TCO parity today would require more than $330,000 in purchase incentives for Class 8 fleet operators. Lower-priced vehicles need less, because they start closer to parity. Figure 1 shows how HVIP base vouchers and CFR incentives stack up against the gap for all heavy-duty vehicle classes.
